articles.text: LǏ MÍNG: Zǎoshang hǎo!
LǏ MÍNG: Good morning!
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Zǎoshang hǎo! Nín guìxìng?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Good morning! May I ask your name?
LǏ MÍNG: Wǒ xìng Lǐ, zài Běijīng wǒ jiànguo nín.
LǏ MÍNG: My name is Lǐ. I met you in Běijīng.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Zài Běijīng? Shénme dìfangr?
GAIL GRIFFITH: In Běijīng? Where?
LǏ MÍNG: Qīyuè sìhào wǎnshang, zài Měiguó Dàshǐguǎn.
LǏ MÍNG: On the evening of July fourth, at the American Embassy.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Ā! Qīyuè sìhào, nèitian yǒu nàme duō rén, wǒ bú jìde le. Nín zài nǎr gōngzuò a?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Ah! July fourth. There were so many people that day, I don't remember. Where do you work?
LǏ MÍNG: Wàimàobù. Nèitian, Wàimàobùde gànbu qùle bù shǎo, nín bú huì jìde le. Wǒ hǎoxiàng jìde nín shi gǎo yǔyánxuéde.
LǏ MÍNG: The Ministry of Foreign Trade. That day, a lot of cadres from the Ministry of Foreign Trade went; you wouldn't remember. I seem to remember that you are in linguistics.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Bù zhǐ shi yǔyánxué, wǒ hái yánjiū mínzú wèntí, zhǒngzú wèntí.
GAIL GRIFFITH: Not only linguistics. I also study national and racial issues.
LǏ MÍNG: Ō! Dào Xīnjiāng qù yánjiū mínzú wèntí ma?
LǏ MÍNG: Oh! Are you going to Xīnjiāng to do research on nationalities?
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Bù, wǒ shi xiǎng duō liǎojiě yìdiǎnr Wéiwúěr wénhuà hé Zhōngguó wénhuàde guānxi.
GAIL GRIFFITH: No. I want to get a better understanding of the relationship between Uygur culture and Chinese culture.
LǏ MÍNG: Ō! Zhè kě shi yíge fùzáde wèntí, wǒ bú shi lìshǐ xuéjiā, guānyú zhèige me, wǒ zhīdaode bú tài duō.
LǏ MÍNG: Oh! That's certainly a complex question. I'm not a historian. On that topic...I don't know very much.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Nǐmen zǒng bǐ wǒmen zhīdaode duō, jiù qǐng nín jiǎngjiang ba.
GAIL GRIFFITH: But you know more than we do, in any case, so please tell me about it.
LǏ MÍNG: Wǒ zhīdao cóngqián Wéiwúěr rén yòngde wénzì shi Zhōngdōngde, yìzhí dào xiànzài, zài Xīnjiāng Wéiwúěr Zìzhìqūde xuéxiàoli háishi jiāo Wéiwúěrwén.
LǏ MÍNG: I know that the writing which the Uygurs used to use was Middle Eastern. Even now, they still teach the Uygur language in the schools in the Xīnjiāng Uygur Autonomous Region.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Nàme yǒu duōshǎo Wéiwúěr rén dǒng Hànyǔ ne?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Then how many Uygurs understand Chinese?
LǏ MÍNG: Dàgài bú dào bǎifēnzhī èrshí.
LǏ MÍNG: Probably fewer than twenty percent.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Ǹg, hěn yǒu yìsi, nàme zhèngfǔ zài zìzhìqūde zhèngcè hé nèidì hěn bù tóng ma?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Hm, very interesting. Then is the government's policy in the autonomous region very different from in the interior?
LǏ MÍNG: Wéiwúěr rén dàbùfen xiāngxìn Yīsīlánjiào. Zhōngguó yě shi zōngjiào zìyóude guójiā, suǒyǐ zài zhèngcèshang huì yǒu yìxiē hé nèidì bù tóngde bànfǎ.
LǏ MÍNG: Most Uygurs believe in Islam. China is a country with freedom of religion, too. So in the area of policy, some ways of doing things are different from in the interior.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Ǹg, wǒmen zài huí dào wénzì wèntíshang hǎo bu hǎo?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Mm. Could we go back to the question of the writing?
LǏ MÍNG: Hǎo a!
LǏ MÍNG: Sure!
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Tīngshuō xiànzài Wéiwúěrwén yǒule xīn wénzì le.
GAIL GRIFFITH: I understand that the Uygur language now has a new orthography.
LǏ MÍNG: Yǒu, xīn wénzì shi Yī Jiǔ Qī Wǔ nián kāishǐ yòngde. Zhèizhǒng xīn wénzì xiěqilai bǐjiào róngyi, cóng nèidì lái Xīnjiāngde rén xuéqilai yě róngyide duō.
LǏ MÍNG: Yes, the new orthography began to be used in 1975. It's easier to write, and for people who come to Xīnjiāng from the interior, it's much easier to learn.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Yǒule xīn wénzì yǐhòu Wéiwúěrzú rén juéde zěnmeyàng? Tāmen hěn gāoxìng ma?
GAIL GRIFFITH: What do the Uygur people think now that they have the new orthography? Are they very happy?
LǏ MÍNG: Zhōngguó shi yíge duō mínzúde shèhuìzhǔyì dà jiātíng, Wéiwúěr rénmín yě shi yào tǒngyīde ma! Yǒule xīn wénzì, Hànzú hé shǎoshù mínzúde wénhuà jiāoliú yě róngyiduō le ma!

LǏ MÍNG: China is a socialist family of many nations. The Uygurs want to be unified, too! With the new orthography, cultural exchange between the Hans and the minority nationalities has also become much easier!
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Nǐ shuōde yǒu dàoli. Duì le, nǐ kě bu kěyi gàosu wǒ Xīnjiāng rénkǒude qíngkuàng?
GAIL GRIFFITH: You are right. Oh yes--can you tell me about the population of Xīnjiāng?
LǏ MÍNG: Xiànzài Xīnjiāng yǒu jiǔbǎiwàn rén zuǒyòu, yǐhòu huì gèng duō.
LǏ MÍNG: Xīnjiāng now has approximately nine million people, and there will be even more in the future.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Shǎoshù mínzú yǒu duōshǎo ne?
GAIL GRIFFITH: How many of that number are minority nationalities?
LǏ MÍNG: Chàbuduō qībǎiduō wàn, érqiě zhèi qībǎiduō wàn rénlǐ yǒu shísānge mínzú.
LǏ MÍNG: Somewhere over seven million. And among these seven million people there are thirteen nationalities.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Ō. Xīnjiāng shǎoshù mínzú gēn Hànzúde jiāoliú yǒu duō jiǔ le?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Oh. How long has there been interchange between the minority nationalities of Xīnjiāng and the Han people?

LǏ MÍNG: Xīnjiāng dìqū hé nèidìde jīngjì jiāoliú yǐjīng yǒu jǐqiānniánde lìshǐ le, yòng wénzì xiěxialáide jīngjì wénhuà jiāoliú shi cóng gōngyuán qián liùbǎi nián zuǒyòu kāishǐde. Gōngyuán qián liùshí nián jīngguò jǐcì zhànzhēng yǐhòu Xīnjiāng hé nèidì tǒngyī le, wénhuà, yìshude jiāoliú yě jiù yuè lái yuè duō le.

LǏ MÍNG: Economic interchange between the Xīnjiāng region and the interior has been going on for several thousand years. Economic and cultural interchange which was put down in writing began around 600 B.C. In 60 B.C., after several wars, Xīnjiāng was united with the interior, and there began to be more and more cultural and artistic interchange.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Wǒ tīngshuō jiěfàng yǐhòu yǒu hěn duō rén bān dào Xīnjiāng lái zhù le.
GAIL GRIFFITH: I understand that many people have moved to Xīnjiāng since liberation.

LǏ MÍNG: Yī Jiǔ Wǔ Líng nián, Xīnjiāng hépíng jiěfàng. Jiěfàngjūn dàole zhèli yǐhòu jiù hé zhèige dìfangde nóngmín yìqǐ gǎo jīngjì jiànshè. Yī Jiǔ Liù Èr nián yǐhòu měinián dōu yǒu hěn duō niánqīng rén dào zhèli lái, nèi shíhou biānjiāngde shēnghuó bǐ nèidì chàde duō, xiànzài jiànshède bú cuò le.

LǏ MÍNG: In 1950, Xīnjiāng was peacefully liberated. After the PLA arrived here, they carried on economic construction with the peasants. Since 1962, every year, a lot of young people have come here. Back then, life in the border region was much worse than in the interior; but now, construction has been pretty well carried out.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Nàme zhèixiē jiànshè biānjiāngde niánqīng rén dōu shi cóng nǎr láide ne?
GAIL GRIFFITH: And where have all these young people who are carrying on the construction of the borderlands come from?
LǏ MÍNG: Duōbànr shi Tiānjīn, Běijīng, Shànghǎi, Zhèjiāngde qīngnián.
LǏ MÍNG: Most of them are youth from Tiānjīn, Běijīng, Shànghǎi, and Zhèjiāng.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Tāmen hái kěyi huí dà chéngshì ma?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Can they still go back to the big cities?
LǏ MÍNG: Xiànzài jiāotōng fāngbian, fàng jiàde shíhou tāmen kěyi huí lǎojiā kànkan. Duōbànrde niánqīng rén zài zhèli jiéle hūn, yǒule háizi, tāmen yǐjīng shi Xīnjiāng rén le!

LǏ MÍNG: Now, transportation is convenient, so when they have vacation, they can go back to visit their original home. Most of the young people have married here and have children; they have already become Xīnjiāng natives!
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Tāmen zài zhèli zuò shénme? Jiù gǎo nóngyè ma?
GAIL GRIFFITH: What do they do here? Just farming?
LǏ MÍNG: Ō! Bù dōu shi gǎo nóngyè. Yě yǒude shi gōngren, yě yǒude gǎo wénhuà jiàoyù gōngzuò, hái yǒude gǎo xùmùyè.
LǏ MÍNG: Oh, not all of them. Some are workers, some do cultural and educational work, and some do livestock farming.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Duì le, suīrán Xīnjiāng yǒu hěn dàde shāmò, kěshi xùmùyè hái shi hěn fādáde.
GAIL GRIFFITH: Oh, yes; although Xīnjiāng has a big desert, livestock farming is still very well developed.
LǏ MÍNG: Nǐ jiànguo Xīnjiāngde dìtǎn meiyou?
LǏ MÍNG: Have you ever seen Xīnjiāng carpets?
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Zài zhǎnlǎnhuìshang jiànguo. Tz! Zhēn měi! Duō měide dìtǎn!
GAIL GRIFFITH: At an exhibition. Gee! They're really beautiful! Such beautiful carpets!
LǏ MÍNG: Měinián Xīnjiāng dìqū jiāo gěi guójiā bù shǎo dìtǎn. Tāmende shēngchǎn qíngkuàng bú cuò, shùliàng bù shǎo, zhìliàng yě hěn gāo, wàiguó péngyou hěn xǐhuan mǎi.

LǏ MÍNG: Every year the Xīnjiāng region hands over quite a few carpets to the state. They are doing well in production; they produce quite a number of carpets, and the quality is also very high. Foreign friends love to buy them.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Ā! Wǒ zhīdao le, nǐ shi dào Xīnjiāng qu chūchāide ba!
GAIL GRIFFITH: Ah! Now I know: I bet you're going to Xīnjiāng on business!
LǏ MÍNG: Duì le. Qù hé jǐge dìtǎnchǎng tǎolùn míngniánde shēngchǎn jìhua.
LǏ MÍNG: Right. I'm going to discuss next year's production plan with a few carpet factories.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Zhèixiē dìtǎnchǎng kě bu kěyi cānguān na?
GAIL GRIFFITH: Can one visit these carpet factories?
LǏ MÍNG: Zěnme bù kěyi? Huānyíng huānyíng! Nín hé Lǚxíngshè tányitán, tāmen huì ānpáide.
LǏ MÍNG: Of course! You are very welcome to visit! Talk to the Travel Service about it, and they'll make the arrangements.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Duìbuqǐ, nǐde biǎo xiànzài jǐdiǎn le? Wǒde biǎo hǎoxiàng kuài le.
GAIL GRIFFITH: Excuse me--what time do you have? My watch seems to be fast.
LǏ MÍNG: Zhōngwǔ shí'èrdiǎn.
LǏ MÍNG: Twelve noon.
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Wǒ zěnme juéde tiān liàngle bù jiǔ a.
GAIL GRIFFITH: How come I feel as if it's only been light out for a little while?
LǏ MÍNG: Nín bié wàng le, zhèrde shíjiān hé Běijīng chà sìge zhōngtóu ne!
LǏ MÍNG: Don't forget, there's a four-hour time difference between here and Běijīng!
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Zěnme chà sìge zhōngtóu?
GAIL GRIFFITH: How is that?
LǏ MÍNG: Zài Běijīng qīdiǎn zhōng tiān jiù liàng le, zài zhèr Běijīng shíjiān shíyīdiǎn tiān cái liàng ne!
LǏ MÍNG: In Běijīng it gets light at seven o'clock. Here, it doesn't get light until eleven o'clock Běijīng time!

GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Duìle, duìle... Ōu, quánguó dōu tǒngyīde yòng Běijīng shíjiān ma? Zhè hé Měiguó bù yíyàng, Měiguó yǒu sìge shíjiān ne.... Xiànzài wǒmen yǐjīng zài huǒchēshang guòle qīshíge zhōngtóu le! Shénme shíhour kěyi dào Wūlǔmùqí ya?

GAIL GRIFFITH: I see, I see...hm, Běijīng time is used throughout the country? That's different from America. America has four times.... Now we've already spent seventy hours on the train! What time will we get to Ürümqi?
LǏ MÍNG: Hái yǒu bāge zhōngtóu ne. Hǎo le, zhànlèi le ba, wǒ gāi huíqu xiūxi yìhuǐr le. Huí tóur jiàn!
LǏ MÍNG: We still have another eight hours. Well, you must be tired of standing up. I should go back and rest a bit. See you later!
GÀI'ĚR GÉLǏFÚSĪ: Huí tóur jiàn, Lǐ Xiānsheng.
GAIL GRIFFITH: See you later, Mr. Lǐ.
